extracted.intended_audience: general readers and mathematicians interested in number theory (students, researchers, enthusiasts)
extracted.subtask_description: A Wikipedia article describing the definition, elementary properties, theorems, conjectures, empirical results and recent progress related to twin primes (prime pairs differing by two). It summarizes known results (Brun, Zhang, Goldston–Pintz–Yıldırım, Maynard), conjectures (twin prime, Hardy–Littlewood, Polignac) and computational records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of twin prime
rubrics_metrics.description: A twin prime is a prime number that is either 2 less or 2 more than another prime number; sometimes the term refers to the pair (prime twin / prime pair).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: (17, 19), (41, 43). Usually the pair (2,3) is not considered a twin prime pair because 2 is the only even prime. Equivalent formulation: a prime with prime gap 2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form (6n−1, 6n+1) for twin primes (> (3,5))
rubrics_metrics.description: Every twin prime pair greater than (3,5) is of the form (6n−1, 6n+1) for some natural number n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequence: the number between the two primes is a multiple of 6; the sum of any such twin prime pair (other than (3,5)) is divisible by 12. Five is the only prime that belongs to two twin pairs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Twin prime conjecture
rubrics_metrics.description: Conjecture that there are infinitely many primes p such that p+2 is also prime (the k=1 case of de Polignac's conjecture).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This remains unsolved. The conjecture is implied by stronger conjectures such as the first Hardy–Littlewood conjecture (prime k‑tuples) and has relations to other hypotheses (e.g., certain strengthenings of Goldbach or existence of Siegel zeros).

rubrics_metrics.name: Brun's theorem (convergence of reciprocals)
rubrics_metrics.description: The sum of the reciprocals of the twin primes converges (Brun's theorem).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduced the Brun sieve and Brun's constant; implies twin primes are 'sparse' enough for the reciprocal sum to converge. Used to derive upper bounds on the counting function of twin primes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Upper bound on count of twin primes
rubrics_metrics.description: The number of twin primes less than N does not exceed C·N/(log N)^2 for some absolute constant C>0; more refined bounds involve the twin prime constant C2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A refined form given in the article: (8 C2 N / (log N)^2)[1 + O((log log N)/(log N))], where C2 is the twin prime constant (≈0.6601618...). This is an upper bound, not an asymptotic equality.

rubrics_metrics.name: First Hardy–Littlewood conjecture (asymptotic for π2(x))
rubrics_metrics.description: Conjecture that the number π2(x) of primes p ≤ x with p+2 prime satisfies π2(x) ~ 2 C2 x/(ln x)^2 as x→∞.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines the twin prime constant C2 = ∏_{p≥3} (1 − 1/(p−1)^2) ≈ 0.6601618158.... Justification heuristic: assume prime density ≈ 1/ln t (from the prime number theorem). The article notes the second Hardy–Littlewood conjecture is believed false and the full k‑tuple conjecture implies extensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polignac's conjecture (generalization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conjecture (1849) that for every positive even integer k there are infinitely many consecutive prime pairs p, p' with p'−p = k (so k=2 is the twin prime conjecture).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not proven for any specific k. Zhang's result implies at least one even k exists with infinitely many prime gaps equal to k (bounded gaps result), so Polignac's conjecture would follow only if shown for every even k.

rubrics_metrics.name: Zhang's bounded gaps theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: There exists an integer N (< 70 million in Zhang's original 2013 result) such that infinitely many pairs of primes differ by at most N; subsequent work reduced the bound (to 246 in the literature cited).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This was a major breakthrough toward twin-prime-type results. Polymath and independent work (Maynard, Tao) improved the bounds; assuming the Elliott–Halberstam conjecture (and generalized forms) would further lower the bound to 12 or 6.

rubrics_metrics.name: Goldston–Pintz–Yıldırım small gaps results
rubrics_metrics.description: Results showing there is a constant c<1 and infinitely many primes p with next prime p' satisfying p'−p < c·ln p (and later improvements showing c can be arbitrarily small): lim inf (p_{n+1}−p_n)/ln p_n = 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These theorems show the existence of infinitely many pairs of primes with gaps growing much slower than typical gaps; they do not by themselves imply infinitely many gaps equal to 2 but demonstrate progress toward small gaps results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chen prime (lower member) and prime triplets
rubrics_metrics.description: The lower member m of a twin prime pair (m, m+2) is by definition a Chen prime; if m−4 or m+6 is also prime then the three primes form a prime triplet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chen primes are an established concept; the article notes relationships among twin primes, prime triplets, and other k‑tuples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factorial congruence characterisation of twin pairs
rubrics_metrics.description: A pair (m, m+2) is a twin prime pair iff 4((m−1)! + 1) ≡ −m (mod m(m+2)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a proven elementary congruence criterion cited in the article; useful as an explicit arithmetic characterization (but not a practical primality test).

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrictions on n (mod primes) for 6n±1 pattern
rubrics_metrics.description: For a twin pair of the form (6n−1, 6n+1), the integer n must avoid residues that make one of the pair divisible by small primes (e.g., ending digits that would make one member a multiple of 5).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: n ending in 1 or 6 makes 6n−1 divisible by 5 (unless n=1). More generally, modulo any prime p ≥ 5, if n ≡ ±6^{−1} (mod p) one member will be divisible by p; this restricts allowable n for twin primes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical distribution and limiting constant behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical analyses show the normalized count f(x) in f(x)·x/(log x)^2 is about 1.7 for small x and decreases toward about 1.3 as x grows; conjecturally the limit equals 2·C2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This summarizes computational/empirical evidence up to large ranges; relates observed data to the Hardy–Littlewood conjectured asymptotic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Large twin primes and computational records
rubrics_metrics.description: Distributed computing projects (Twin Prime Search, PrimeGrid) have found record-largest twin primes (e.g., a 388,342-digit pair discovered in 2016); there are many twin pairs below large thresholds (e.g., counts below 10^18).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article cites specific record pairs, project names, and counts; these are computational/empirical achievements rather than theoretical results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Isolated prime (non-twin) and density statement
rubrics_metrics.description: An isolated prime (also called single or non-twin prime) is a prime p such that neither p−2 nor p+2 is prime; Brun's theorem implies that almost all primes are isolated in the sense that their proportion tends to 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples listed (2, 23, 37, ...). The density statement follows from the convergence of the sum of reciprocals of twin primes and the sparsity that implies.
